\title{Sub-Riemannian geoemtry}

\section{Sub-Riemannian manifolds}
Let $M^{m+k}$ be a $(m+k)$-dimensional smooth manifold and $\mathcal{H}^m$ be  a  subbundle of $TM$ of rank $m$. Assume that $\mathcal{H}$ satisfies step-$r$ bracket generating condition for some $r \geq 1$.
This means that, at each point \( x \in M \), the sections of \( \mathcal{H} \), along with all their Lie brackets up to order \( r \), generate the tangent space \( T_xM \).
Then the triple $(M^{m+k},\mathcal{H}^m,g_{\mathcal{H}})$ is called a sub-Riemannian manifold, where $g_{\mathcal{H}}$ is a fiberwise metric on $\mathcal{H}$. The subbundle $\mathcal{H}$ is also called the \textit{horizontal distribution}. Note that one can easily extend $g_{\mathcal{H}}$ to a Riemannian metric $g$ on $TM$ (see, e.g., \cite{dongEellsSampsonType2021a}). Throughout the paper, we fix such a metric $g$ such that $g|_{\mathcal{H}}=g_{\mathcal{H}}$ and denote the corresponding sub-Riemannian manifold by $(M^{m+k},\mathcal{H}^{m},g)$. 
The term ``complete'' as it applies to $(M, \mathcal{H}, g)$ will refer to the Riemannian metric $g$ being complete.
Now $TM$ admits a direct sum decomposition
$$ TM=\mathcal{H} \oplus \mathcal{V}, $$       
where \( \mathcal{V} \) denotes the \textit{vertical distribution}, namely the orthogonal complement of \( \mathcal{H} \) with respect to the metric \( g \).  
Then 
we have the natural projections
$$ \pi _{\mathcal{H}}:TM \to \mathcal{H}, \quad  \pi _{\mathcal{V}}:TM \to \mathcal{V}.$$
We denote by $\mathfrak{X},\mathfrak{X}_{\mathcal{H}},\mathfrak{X}_{\mathcal{V}}$ the spaces of all smooth sections of  $TM$,  $\mathcal{H}$ and  $\mathcal{V}$, respectively. 



When dealing with $L^p$-vanishing results on sub-Riemannian manifolds, the  notion of  generalized Sobolev spaces  introduced by  Rothschild and Stein \cite{Rothstein1976hyp} is useful. Let $(M^{m+k},\mathcal{H}^m,g)$ be a sub-Riemannian manifold, and $U \subset M$ be a coordinate neighborhood on which a horizontal  frame   $\{e_1,\dots,e_m\}$ is defined. The generalized Sobolev spaces
is defined as 
$$ S_{l}^{p}(U)=\left\{ u \in L^p(U)|e_{i_1} \cdots e_{i_s}(u) \in L^p(U), 1 \leq i_{1} \leq \cdots \leq i_s \leq m, 0 \leq s \leq l \right\}. $$
These notions can be easily extended to any relatively compact domain. 

Next, we recall some examples of sub-Riemannian manifolds.

\begin{example}[Riemannian foliations]   
	Let  $(M^{m+k},\mathcal{F}^k)$ be a foliated manifold,
	 where $\mathcal{F}^k$ is  a $k$-dimensional foliation. Let $g$ be a Riemannian metric on $M$ and decompose the tangent bundle 
	 $$ TM=T\mathcal{F} \oplus \mathcal{H} $$ 
	 accordingly, where $\mathcal{H}$ is  complementary to $T\mathcal{F} $. The metric $g$ is said to be bundle-like if the Lie derivate of $g_{\mathcal{H}}$ along vertical direction vanishes. 
	 Geometrically, this condition implies that the foliation arises locally from a Riemannian submersion.    
	The triple $(M^{m+k},\mathcal{F}^k,g)$ is referred to as a \textit{Riemannian foliation}, see  \cite{CDHL2026hor} or \cite{gromollMetricFoliationsCurvature2009a} for more details. 
	When $\mathcal{H}$ is bracket generating, $(M^{m+k},\mathcal{H}^m,g)$ is a sub-Riemannian manifold.  
\end{example}

Carnot groups are typical examples in sub-Riemannian geometry. Moreover, they can be endowed with a bundle-like metric structure, see \cite{Baudoin2025sub}.
\begin{example}[Carnot groups]\label{exCar}
	 A Carnot group is a simply connected Lie group $G$  whose Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}$ admits a stratified decomposition: 
	$$ \mathfrak{g}=V_1 \oplus V_2 \oplus \cdots \oplus V_r \quad (r \geq 1) $$
	such that $[V_1,V_j]=V_{j+1}$ for $1 \leq j \leq r-1$ and $[V_1,V_r]=\{0\}$.   This gives a Lie algebra grading 
	\begin{equation}\label{31}
		[V_i,V_j] \subset V_{i+j}, 
	\end{equation}
	where $V_j:=\{0\}$ for $j >r$.  Define a distribution $\mathcal{H}$ on $G$ by 
	$$ \mathcal{H}_x=dL_{x}(V_1) \subset T_xG, \quad \forall  x \in G .$$ 
	Here $L_x$ is the left translation of $G$ relative to  $x$.   
	Let $g_{\mathcal{H}}$ be a left-invariant metric on $\mathcal{H}$.  We can extend $g_{\mathcal{H}}$ to a Riemannian metric $g$  such that  $V_i \perp V_j$ for $i \neq j$. Then $(G,\mathcal{H},g)$ is a step-$r$  sub-Riemannian manifold. Thus 
	we have  decomposition:
	$$ TG=\mathcal{H} \oplus \mathcal{V} .$$
	Since $[\mathcal{V}, \mathcal{V}] \subset  \mathcal{V}$, $\mathcal{V}$  is the vertical bundle of a foliation $\mathcal{F}$  on $G$.  
\end{example}

\begin{example}[Contact  manifolds, cf. \cite{Bla2010rie}]\label{excont}
	Let $M^{2m+1}$  be a contact  manifold with  structure tensors $( \phi  , \mathsf{T}  , \theta   , g)$. 
	Precisely speaking, $\theta $ is a contact form (i.e., $\theta \wedge (d \theta)^m \neq 0$), $\mathsf{T}$ is the Reeb vector field, $\phi $ is a $(1,1)$-tensor and $g$ is a Riemannian metric  such that  
	\begin{equation}\label{2}
		 \begin{cases}
			\phi ^2=-I+\theta \otimes \mathsf{T}, \quad \phi (\mathsf{T})=0, \quad \theta (\mathsf{T})=1; &\text{}\\
			g(\phi X,\phi Y) = g(X,Y)-\theta (X)\theta (Y), &\text{} \forall X,Y \in TM;\\
			g(X,\phi Y)=d \theta (X,Y),&\text{} \forall X,Y \in TM.
		\end{cases}  
	\end{equation}   
	The vertical and horizontal distributions are given by $\mathcal{V}:=\Span_{\rr} \{\mathsf{T}\} $ and $\mathcal{H}:=\ker \theta  $. It follows from the last equality of \eqref{2} that $\mathcal{H}$ is step-$2$ bracket generating, hence $(M^{2m+1},\mathcal{H}^{2m},g)$ is a sub-Riemannian manifold.   
\end{example}

\begin{example}[Pseudo-Hermitian manifolds]
	Let $M$ be a real $(2m+p)$-dimensional oriented manifold. A \textit{CR structure} of type $(m,p)$ is a complex subbundle   $H^{1,0}$  of   $TM \otimes \cc$, of complex rank $m$,   satisfying the (formally) integrable condition. The pair $(M,H^{1,0})$ is  called a  \textit{CR manifold of type $(m,p)$}.  Set $H^{0,1}=\overline{H^{1,0}}$.
	Alternatively,  the CR structure can  be described by a pair $(\mathcal{H},J_b)$, where $\mathcal{H} $ is the real bundle $\Re\{H^{1,0} \oplus H^{0,1}\}$  and $J_b$ is its almost complex structure defined by $J_b(X+\overline{X})=\sqrt{-1}(X-\overline{X})$ for all $X \in H^{1,0}$.   
	
	Let us consider the special case that $(M,H^{1,0})$ is   a  CR manifold of type $(m,1)$, which is also referred as \textit{hypersurface type} (see \cite[\S 1.1]{DT2006differential} for details).      
	Since $M$ is oriented, there is a $1$-form $\theta $ which annihilates $\mathcal{H}$. Define the Levi form $L_{\theta }$  by 
	$$ L_\theta (X,Y)=d \theta (X,J_b Y), \quad \forall  X,Y \in \mathfrak{X}_{\mathcal{H}} . $$    
	When  $L_\theta $ is positive definite on $\mathcal{H}$, the CR manifold $(M,H^{1,0})$ is  said to be  \textit{strictly pseudoconvex} and  the triple $(M^{2m+1},\mathcal{H},\theta )$ is called a \textit{pseudo-Hermitian manifold}. This also implies that $\mathcal{H}$ is step-$2$  bracket generating.    Clearly, $\theta $ is a contact form and there is a unique Reeb vector field $\mathsf{T} $  satisfying 
	$$ \theta (\mathsf{T} )=1, \quad i_{\mathsf{T}}(d \theta) =0. $$  
	The collection of all its integral curves forms an oriented one-dimensional foliation $\mathcal{V}$  on $M$, which is called the \textit{Reeb foliation}.
	Define $J$ as  the extension of  $J_b$ to $TM$  satisfying $J(\mathsf{T})=0$. 
	Then there is a canonical metric called \textit{Webster metric} on $M$, given by 
	$$ g=L_{\theta }+\theta \otimes \theta . $$  
	Now $\mathcal{V}$ is the orthogonal complementary of $\mathcal{H}$ with respect to $g$.   
	Note that $g(JX,JY)=g(X,Y)$ for all $X,Y \in \mathfrak{X}_{\mathcal{H}}$. Obviously, $(M^{2m+1},\mathcal{H},g)$ is a sub-Riemannian manifold. There are two natural connections on a pseudo-Hermitian manifold, the Levi-Civita connection $\nabla $ and the Tanaka-Webster connection $\nabla ^{TW}$. It's known that $\nabla ^{TW}$ is   compatible with the CR structure and the metric. The \textit{pseudo-Hermitian torsion} of $\nabla ^{TW}$, denoted by  $\tau $, is given by 
	$$ \tau (X)=T_{\nabla ^{TW}}(\mathsf{T},X) $$
	for all $X \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$, where $T_{\nabla ^{TW}}$ is the torsion tensor of $\nabla ^{TW}$.   The pseudo-Hermitian manifold $(M^{2m+1},\mathcal{H},\theta )$ is called \textit{Sasakian} if $\tau =0$.    
	 For more information about pseudo-Hermitian geometry we refer the reader to  \cite{DT2006differential} or \cite{CDRY2019onharm}.       
\end{example}




In  \cite{Bej1978Cr}, A. Bejancu introduced the notion of CR-submanifolds, which serve as an intermediate class between complex submanifolds and totally real submanifolds in  complex differential geometry.
\begin{example}[CR-submanifolds, cf. \cite{bej1986}]\label{exCrsub}
	Let $(M,g)$ be a submanifold of a Hermitian manifold $(\widetilde{M},J,\tilde{g})$, where $g$ is the induced metric on $M$ from $\tilde{g}$. 
	The submanifold $M$ is called a \textit{CR-submanifold} in $\widetilde{M}$ if there is a $C^{\infty}$ distribution $\mathcal{H}$ on $M$ satisfying the following conditions: 
	(i) $J(\mathcal{H}_x)= \mathcal{H}_x$ for each $x \in M$; (ii) $J(\mathcal{V}_x) \subset T_{x}^{\perp}M$ for each $x\in M$, 
	where $\mathcal{V}$ is the orthogonal complement  of $\mathcal{H}$ in $TM$ according to $g$, 
	and $T^{\perp}M$ is the normal bundle of $M$ in $\widetilde{M}$. Let $2m$ and $p$ denote the ranks of $\mathcal{H}$ and $\mathcal{V}$ respectively. 
	Then it follows from \cite[Theorem 4.1]{BlCh1979cr} that $(M,\mathcal{H},J|_{\mathcal{H}})$ is a CR manifold of type $(m,p)$. We remark, however, that the induced metric $g$ (in the case  $p=1$) doesn't coincide with the Webster metric in general. If  $\mathcal{H}$ satisfies bracket generating condition, then $(M,\mathcal{H},g)$ is a sub-Riemannian manifold.   
\end{example}

\section{Bott connection}
It would be convenient to introduce a suitable linear connection compatible with
the sub-Riemannian structure on $(M,H,g_H;g)$ in some sense. The generalized Bott
connection is one of such connections given by
\[
\nabla^{\mathfrak B}_X Y
=
\begin{cases}
\pi_H\bigl(\nabla^R_XY\bigr),
& X,Y\in\Gamma(H),\\[4pt]
\pi_H\bigl([X,Y]\bigr),
& X\in\Gamma(V),\ Y\in\Gamma(H),\\[4pt]
\pi_V\bigl([X,Y]\bigr),
& X\in\Gamma(H),\ Y\in\Gamma(V),\\[4pt]
\pi_V\bigl(\nabla^R_XY\bigr),
& X,Y\in\Gamma(V).
\end{cases}
\]

where $\nabla^R$ denotes the Riemannian connection of $g$. Clearly,
$\nabla^{B}$ preserves the decomposition, and it also satisfies
\[
\nabla^{B}_X g_H=0
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\nabla^{B}_Y g_V=0
\]
for any $X\in H$ and $Y\in V$. However, $\nabla^{B}$ does \textit{not} preserve the Riemannian metric $g$ in general.

\begin{lemma}
For any \(X,Y\in\Gamma(TM)\), we have
\[
T(X,Y)
=
-\pi_V\bigl([\pi_H(X),\pi_H(Y)]\bigr)
-\pi_H\bigl([\pi_V(X),\pi_V(Y)]\bigr).
\]
\end{lemma}
